notes.meaning: The thirteenth day of the month of Adar arrived, which was the date Haman had chosen by casting lots to wipe out the Jews. Their enemies hoped to overpower them on that day, but God reversed the situation so that the Jews overcame those who hated them instead. When God steps in, the very day meant for disaster can turn into a day of deliverance.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Few modern historians view the events of Esther as literal history, often questioning whether an empire-wide battle could have taken place without Persian records mentioning it.

notes.meaning: Across all the Persian provinces, the Jews banded together in their cities to fight against anyone trying to harm them. No one could stand against them because terror struck the hearts of the local populations. God put a deep dread into their attackers, allowing the Jewish people to prevail.

All the provincial rulers, governors, and royal administrators gave active help to the Jews. They did this because they were in awe of Mordecai, who was now second in rank to the king. Seeing that the palace and the law backed the Jews, the officers knew it was dangerous to oppose them.

Mordecai exercised great influence within the king's palace, and news of his power spread throughout the empire. He grew steadily more respected and powerful as he served with wisdom. When God lifts up a godly leader, that leader's influence brings safety and blessing to others.

The Jews struck down their enemies with swords and weapons, defeating all who came out to kill them. They had complete victory and did as they pleased to their attackers. This was a lawful act of self-defense against people who had joined Haman's plot to murder them.

In the citadel of Susa, the royal quarter of the capital, the Jews killed five hundred men. These were not palace servants, but armed supporters of Haman who lived in the city around the palace. Even close to the king's court, an angry faction had organized an attack against the Jewish people.

The account lists the names of Haman's ten sons: Parshandatha, Dalphon, Aspatha, Poratha, Adalia, Aridatha, Parmashta, Arisai, Aridai, and Vaizatha. These brothers had likely led the five hundred attackers in Susa to avenge their father. With their deaths, the family that had tried to destroy the Jews lost all its power and standing.

The Jews killed all ten sons of Haman, but they did not take any of their goods or property. The king's decree allowed them to take plunder, but they deliberately refused it. This made it clear to everyone that they were fighting solely for their lives, not out of greed.

On that very day, officials reported the number of people killed in the citadel of Susa directly to the king. Xerxes stayed informed about the fighting to maintain order in his capital. Accurate reports helped the king understand how deep Haman's conspiracy had run.

Xerxes told Queen Esther that five hundred men and Haman's ten sons had fallen in Susa alone, wondering how many more must have died across the empire. Instead of being angry, the king offered to grant Esther any further request she might have. He showed complete support for the queen and wanted her people to be safe.

Esther asked for the Jews in Susa to be allowed one more day of self-defense and for the bodies of Haman's ten sons to be hung on the gallows. She made this request because many dangerous conspirators had gone into hiding and would attack again if left alone. Hanging the dead bodies of the ten sons was a public warning to terrify anyone thinking of harming the Jews.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some critical writers argue that Esther's plea for another day was unnecessary and reflected personal vengeance rather than self-defense.

notes.meaning: The king approved Esther's request and published an order across Susa extending the decree for another day. Then the bodies of Haman's ten sons were publicly hung up on the gallows. This public act showed the whole city that the plot against the Jews had failed completely.

On the fourteenth day of Adar, the Jews in Susa gathered once more and killed three hundred enemies who had hidden from the first day's fighting. Just as before, they refused to touch any of the plunder. They maintained the high moral ground by showing their only concern was protecting their community.

Across the other provinces of the empire, the Jews gathered to defend themselves and won relief from their attackers. They struck down seventy-five thousand of their enemies, yet they took no plunder at all. By refusing the spoils, they proved they were carrying out self-defense rather than theft.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note that early Greek manuscripts give a smaller count of 15,000, or suggest the Hebrew term for thousands can refer to extended family units rather than individual fighters.

notes.meaning: The Jews in the provinces completed their fighting on the thirteenth day of Adar. On the fourteenth day, they rested from conflict and turned the day into a celebration filled with feasting and joy. They paused from their struggle to give thanks for the life and safety God had granted them.

The Jews in the capital city of Susa fought on both the thirteenth and fourteenth days of Adar to finish clearing out their enemies. Because of this extra day, they rested on the fifteenth day, making it their time of feasting and joy. Their schedule differed slightly from the provinces because of the ongoing danger in the citadel.

Because the provincial Jews finished early, those living in unwalled country villages kept the fourteenth of Adar as their regular holiday of rejoicing, feasting, and sending gifts of food. Sharing food portions was an Eastern custom to include the poor and those grieving at home. It helped everyone share in the relief and celebration.

Mordecai recorded these remarkable events and sent official letters to all the Jews across every province of the Persian empire. He wanted every Jewish family, whether near or far, to preserve the story of their rescue. Putting God's mighty acts into writing ensures that His faithfulness is never forgotten.

Mordecai told the people to celebrate both the fourteenth and fifteenth days of Adar every year. These were the days they found rest from their enemies, when their sorrow turned into joy and their mourning became a feast. He told them to mark the season with feasting, sending gifts of food to friends, and giving generously to the poor.

The Jews throughout the empire agreed to continue the yearly celebration they had begun, just as Mordecai had written. They willingly bound themselves to keep the festival alive for future generations. Remembering God's rescue became a lasting joy shared by the whole community.

These verses summarize why the festival was established: Haman had plotted to wipe out the Jews and had cast the lot (called the Pur) to pick the day for their death. But when the plot was exposed before the king, Xerxes issued written orders that Haman's wicked scheme should fall back on his own head, leading to him and his sons being hanged on the gallows. God used the very trap set by the enemy to bring down the persecutors.

Because of Haman's lots, the people named the new festival Purim, from the Persian word for lot. They kept these days faithfully because of Mordecai's letter and because of what they had seen with their own eyes. The name was a reminder that God, not random chance, directs the outcome of all events.

The Jews bound themselves, their descendants, and all gentiles who converted to their faith to observe these two days without fail every year. Every family, province, and city was to remember Purim so that its memory would never fade among them. Keeping the memory of God's deliverance alive helps every new generation stand firm in faith.

Queen Esther and Mordecai wrote with full royal authority to confirm a second letter regarding the festival of Purim. While Mordecai's earlier letter had recommended the feast, this joint decree established it as an official law for the whole nation. Esther used her royal position to ensure her people's deliverance would always be celebrated.

Mordecai sent letters carrying words of peace and truth to all the Jews across the one hundred twenty-seven provinces of the empire. The letters confirmed the dates of Purim, along with the times of fasting and crying out to God that the people had pledged to observe in memory of their trouble. Remembering their past tears made their celebration of God's answer all the more joyful.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note that the ancient Greek translation lacks the phrase mentioning fasting and cries of lamentation, suggesting it may have entered the Hebrew text as an explanatory note.

notes.meaning: Esther's royal decree gave full legal standing to the rules for Purim, and the account was written down in the official records. The feast was now a permanent part of the Jewish calendar and royal history. Writing down God's wonders keeps His faithfulness clear before our eyes for all time.

other.label: Catholic and Orthodox
other.view: Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include additional Greek passages in Esther that expand the ending and add explicit prayers and mentions of God throughout the book.
